body.p: Applicant has reviewed the final Office action dated August 27, 2024, and the references cited therein. Claims 1-13 and 16 are currently pending. Claim 16 is withdrawn from consideration. Claims 1-13 stand rejected. Claims 14-15 are canceled. Claim 16 is withdrawn from examination.
Applicant's Amendments

Applicant, in view of the continued rejection of Applicant's previously amended claims over the combined teachings of the Mahajan and Mesin references, has amended independent claim 1 to emphasize/highlight features distinguishing over the cited prior art teachings. The amendments include, among other things, the specific clarification that "the electrode arrangement is an electrocardiographic-electromyographic electrode arrangement." See e.g.,
Applicant's original specification at page 12, lines 7-11.

In particular, claim 1 has been amended to emphasize that electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm (which itself already distinguishes from expansion measurements) is performed "using only the first electric signal indicative of the membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm and the second electric signal indicative of the further electric physiologic signals from the body. " See e.g., Applicant's original specification at page 12, lines 6-21.

Furthermore, claim 1 specifies that "the human body is a baby" and further recites that the belt of the carrier "has a length within a range of 100 to 600 millimeter to fit around an abdominal part of a body of the baby"(per now-canceled dependent claim 13). The incorporation of the specified range of length distinguishes Applicant's disclosed/claimed invention over belts that are clearly not suitable for carrying out the functionality of Applicant's currently claimed invention (i.e., performing an electrocardiographic-electromyographic procedure on a baby). Grounds for Rejecting the Claims

1. Claims 1-5 and 11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Mahajan, WO 2015175904 (Mahajan) in view of Mesin (NPL; Separation of propagating and nonpropagating components in surface EMG).
2. Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and Mesin and in view of McGrane, U.S. Pub. No. 2017/0019988 (McGrane).
3. Claim 7 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and Mesin and in view of Maesani, U.S. Pub. No. 2017/0273590 (Maesani).
4. Claims 8 and 10 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over
Mahajan in view of Mesin and Maesani as applied to claim 7 and in further view of Muccio, U.S. Pub. No. 2012/0016440 (Muccio).
5. Claim 9 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and Mesin in view of Hsiao, U.S. Pub. No. 2012/0265025 (Hsiao).
6. Claim 12 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and Mesin as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Sims, U.S. Pub. No. 2007/0293781 (Sims).
7. Claim 13 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Mahajan and
Mesin as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Tupin, U.S. Pub. No. 2011/0060215 (Tupin).

Applicant, in view of at least the current further amendments to claim 1, traverses the grounds for each and every rejection for at least the reasons set forth herein below. Applicant addresses the specific rejections in the order they arise in the Office Action.
Applicant's Specific Responses to the Grounds for Rejection
1. Rejection of Claims 1-5 and 11 as being obvious over Mahajan in view of Mesin

Applicant, at least in view of the current further amendments to independent claim 1, traverses the rejection of claims 1-5 and 11, as being obvious over the combined teachings of Mahajan and Mesin. A proper case of obviousness cannot be established with regard to any one of the currently pending claims since the teachings of the cited Mahajan and Mesin references cannot be combined in a manner that results in Applicant's currently claimed invention.
Moreover, a proper reason cannot be established for one skilled in the art to modify Mahajan's teachings, in view of Mesin, in a way that would result in Applicant's claimed

invention. Notably, none of the references cited in the Office action demonstrates any awareness of a particularized problem that would provide a reason to modify Mahajan (in view of Mesin) in a way that resulted in Applicant's claimed invention.
a. Applicant's Claimed Invention
Applicant's claimed invention is directed to a wearable device including a particular

electrode arrangement that facilitates carrying out electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm of a wearer of the wearable device. In particular currently amended claim 1, provided in clean form below, recites:

body, wherein the human body is a baby, the wearable device comprising:
a carrier comprising a belt, wherein the belt has a length within a range
of 100 to 600 millimeters to fit around an abdominal part of a body of the baby,
and configured to be worn around the body while in use; and
an electrode arrangement comprising a plurality of conductive electrodes

including one or more first electrode and one or more second electrode, wherein the plurality of conductive electrodes are arranged on the carrier to be brought in contact with a skin of the body in use, and wherein the electrode arrangement is an electrocardiographic-electromyographic electrode arrangement wherein all
electrodes of the plurality of conductive electrodes are configured for operating simultaneously to receive electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling

contact with a side part of a torso of the body near the thoracic diaphragm, the one

and for providing the first electrical signal as a measurement signal;

electrical signal using the second electrical signal for enabling
electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm using only the first electric signal indicative of the membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm and the second
electric signal indicative of the further electric physiologic signals from the
body. (Emphasis added).

Thus, Applicant's claimed invention, as presented in further-clarified independent claim 1, recites a wearable device that is particularly configured (including specific sizing of a belt length) for performing electromyography of a thoracic diaphragm of a baby.
Importantly, in a point of distinction in Applicant's previous amendment that was not
addressed in the final Office action, Applicant's disclosed/claimed invention includes the feature:
all electrodes of the plurality of conductive electrodes are configured for
operating simultaneously to receive electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling monitoring of a membrane potential of one or more muscles in the body,

As such, the thoracic diaphragm signal can be provided based solely on EMG signals, through the use of particularized/intelligent filtering of the multiple/simultaneously received EMG signals. This aspect of Applicant's disclosed/claimed invention is not present in any of the cited references' teachings.

Additionally, Applicant's claim 1 has been further amended to emphasize that the belt is designed to monitor babies outside an incubator. In particular, the disclosed/claimed invention is particularly advantageously applied to monitoring breathing of preterm babies by:
(1) obviating a need for adhesive electrodes on fragile newborn infant skin (see, Applicant's specification at page 3, line 28 to page 4, line 2); and
(2) enabling such newborn infants to stay with their mother (see Applicant's specification at page 5, lines 14-25).
b. The cited references do not, in combination, render Applicant's claimed invention
Applicant, at least in view of the current further clarifying amendment to independent claim 1 discussed herein above, traverses the rejection of independent claim 1.

Mahajan, upon which the current rejection of independent claim 1 primarily relies, describes a device that does not obtain a diaphragmatic EMG signal. Rather, Mahajan describes measurement of thoracic motion and thoracic volume which, according to paragraph [0070], relates to a thoracic and diaphragmatic breathing profile. Paragraph [0070] explains that the diaphragmatic breathing profile is determined using thoracic and diaphragmatic expansion sensors.
The final Office action, in the "Response to Arguments", states:
of diagnostic capabilities" in Par 0069. The Examiner's position is that Par 0069 explicitly
teaches the function of performing EMG of a thoracic diaphragm. Further, Mahajan discloses all
of the necessary structure to perform the claimed function (see MPEP 2114). Therefore, the
previous rejection would still stand.
Paragraph [0069], reproduced herein below, states the following:
[0069] The system and methods detailed above may also assess pressures
and blood flow in cardiac chambers for management of heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, assessment of hypovolemia, etc. Chest wall and
5 diaphragmatic movement may also be assessed, along with selective
assessment muscular effort and pattern of chest wall vs. diaphragmatic motion in conjunction with cardio-respiratory indicators for further enhancement of diagnostic capabilities.

However, paragraph [0069] simply does not refer to/describe performing EMG (especially in the diaphragm. Rather Mahajan simply/only describes using "expansion measurement systems" in paragraph [0070] that states the following: [0070] The system is configured to assess respiratory rate and patterns of
10 breathing, and allow for recognition of patterns of breathing that serve as

early indicators of respiratory compromise, along with Integrated and distributed thoracic volume and synchronization of volume change. The system may include one or more of: acoustic monitoring arrays, localization, dry contact EMG, etc. The system may also include thoracic 15 and diaphragmatic expansion sensors located at upper and lower

abdomen, respectively. These sensors may be based on measurement of strain or other variables beneficial for detection of such expansion through measurement of changes in girth or displacement of the upper and lower abdomen. The data from these sensors that include one, two, or more 20 expansion measurement systems may be combined to determine relative
changes associated with thoracic and diaphragmatic breathing profile for determination of pulmonary condition.
As such, one skilled in the art, in view of Mahajan's teachings, would not receive any

teaching/suggestion whatsoever regarding performing EMG on the diaphragm - let alone how to address the specific problems of performing EMG on the diaphragm of a baby (e.g., a relatively very weak signal). As such, Mahajan does not even remotely contemplate Applicant's specific solution of using a second EMG signal from the mid-front of a baby's abdomen to facilitate filtering, and there is no reasonable basis for modifying Mahajan's apparatus in a way that results in Applicant's claimed invention.
Applicant has now further amended independent claim 1 to specify that, among other distinguishing features, the claimed apparatus is particularly configured to be used to monitor breathing of a baby.

Moreover, as noted previously by Applicant in the previous response, Mahajan in paragraph [0070] refers to "diaphragmatic expansion sensors" that perform a "measurement of strain." Such strain measurements enable sensing diaphragmatic expansion by "measurement of changes in girth or displacement of the upper and lower abdomen." Mahajan, indeed, mentions EMG sensors. However Mahajan describes using the EMG sensors to measure organ function drive. See Mahajan, at paragraph [0074]. None of the paragraphs cited in the final Office action [0063], [0070] and [0074] describes using the EMG sensors to provide a diaphragmatic EMG signal output measurement.
On the other hand, the teachings of paragraph [0070] are consistent with the following additional instances of "strain sensor" teachings of Mahajan at:
paragraph [0013]: "a thoracic motion sensor";
paragraph [0016] which states that "chest wall and thoracic volume
monitoring [are sensed] using distributed displacement sensors",
paragraph [0017]: "measurement of thoracic motion and thoracic volume and
lung mechanical response through broadband acoustic methods"
paragraph [0033] which states that "[a]n array of displacement sensors 18
may also be included to measure displacement e.g. of the thoracic cavity."
paragraph [0034]: "thoracic motion array 72";
paragraph [0075]: "thoracic expansion detection";
paragraph [0087]: "measurement of thoracic motion and thoracic volume and
lung mechanical response" (which relates to par. [0017]);
paragraph [00113]: "motion sensors"
paragraphs [00102] and [00120]: "thoracic motion and thoracic volume ".

Applicant adds that claim 1 was previously clarified to recite a combination of features that unequivocally describe Applicant's claimed invention as having first and second conductive electrodes that are of a same type/physical alignment such that both are configured for providing comparable membrane potential signals to facilitate providing the claimed thoracic diaphragmatic EMG signal output measurement.

Mahajan, for a different purpose and unrelated to measuring any thoracic activity, indeed describes EMG sensors at multiple instances. However, none of the instances concerns/suggests using the EMG sensors to measure an EMG of the thoracic diaphragm of a wearer of a wearable device. Moreover, Mahajan never mentions any EMG sensor that directly measures a "membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm" as an electrical signal, in order to perform "electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm" in accordance with Applicant's claimed invention.
The final Office action observes that paragraphs [0070], [0030] and [0087] disclose

multiple sensors that can measure thoracic activity, and asserts that Mahajan thereby anticipates the measuring of "membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm" as an electrical signal. However, such assertion does not properly follow from the noted paragraphs' teachings.

Applicant's claimed structural arrangement facilitates making a direct measurement of a membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm, which enables performing EMG of the thoracic diaphragm. In particular, such direct measurement is made possible by use of the signals of the "second electrodes" to filter the majority of signals of the "first electrodes" to yield the very weak electrical diaphragmatic signals. Thus, Applicant's claimed invention is based on an insight (not mentioned in the cited references) that the shape of the thoracic diaphragm can be used to the benefit of improving measurability and accuracy of EMG measurements on the diaphragmatic movement. See Applicant's FIGs. 2a-c and corresponding description at page 12, line 22 to page 13, line 12.
Moreover, Mahajan's FIG. 1 (showing sensors on a belt), does not disclose Applicant's claimed first and second type electrodes being "aligned on the belt" as in claim 1. The belt in
Mahajan appears to be broad and at best the sensors 16 are aligned, but not with respect to other sensors.

The above shortcomings in Mahajan are not addressed/remedied by the teaching of the cited Mesin reference, upon which the final Office action relies to fill certain admitted shortcomings in the teachings of Mahajan. Mesin appears to present a comprehensive study on a technique for separating propagating and non-propagating components in surface Electromyography (EMG) signals. Mesin describes using an adaptive filter to estimate delays between signals at different channels and to separate the two components. See Mesin, Abstract.
Mesin presents an analysis of surface EMG signals for the purpose of separating

propagating and non-propagating signal components, without reference to respiratory functions or the (thoracic diaphragm) muscles involved in breathing - especially in the context of monitoring breathing of a baby. Mesin does not mention "diaphragm," "thoracic diaphragm," "breathing" or "vital signs", and therefore cannot be reasonably deemed to be directed to Applicant's claimed wearable device that is configured for performing electromyography ojf.a thoracic diaphragm of a baby.

The final Office action refers to an example in Mesin that allegedly describes an EMG device that has a three-electrode array for gathering electrode signals, wherein the electrode signals are processed in order to acquire an accurate EMG signal of a target muscle. This is done in order to test and validate the proposed method for separating the propagating and non- propagating components (e.g. see Mesin, page 131, section 2.5).
For at least the above-provided reasons, Applicant's claimed invention recited in
currently amended independent claim 1 is not rendered obvious by the combined teachings of Mahajan and Mesin.
